title: Mental health first aid and behaviour that challenges
blurb: Respond to acute distress, de-escalate safely and know when (and how) restrictive interventions may be used.
question: Mr Kaminski, 45, is pacing a medical ward corridor and shouting after being told his discharge is delayed. He has not threatened anyone. Other patients look frightened. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

teach.body: De-escalation means using verbal and non-verbal skills to calm a person who is agitated or angry and reduce the risk of violence. A restrictive intervention (restraint, rapid tranquillisation or seclusion) deliberately limits a person's movement or liberty. In plain English: talk first, listen, give space and choices; restriction is a last resort to prevent harm, never a punishment. Behaviour that challenges is often how a person communicates an unmet need such as pain, fear or a full bladder.

steps.label: Spot early signs
steps.sub: Pacing, raised voice, clenched fists, staring

steps.label: Give space
steps.sub: Quiet area, away from others; staff not isolated

steps.label:
Calm body
and voice
steps.sub: Open posture, steady eye contact, respect

steps.label: Offer choices
steps.sub: Avoid flashpoints such as a blunt "no"

teach.caption: Keep trying to de-escalate throughout, including during any restrictive intervention (NG10 rec 1.4.5).

teach.h: Look for the need behind the behaviour
teach.body: When a person with dementia, delirium or a learning disability becomes agitated or hits out, first ask what they might be trying to tell you. NICE CG103 asks you to assess for pain, including non-verbal signs in people with communication difficulties (rec 1.4.9), and to address constipation and dehydration (rec 1.4.5); urinary retention is another common hidden cause of distress. Treating the cause (pain relief, toileting, a familiar routine, glasses or hearing aids) is often what calms the situation.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Kaminski on the corridor
teach.body: One nurse takes the lead. She approaches calmly, keeps a safe distance with an exit behind her, uses his name and says, "I can see this delay is really frustrating. Can we talk about it in the quiet room?" She listens without arguing, explains what she can do (chase the pharmacy, call the doctor) and offers a choice of where to wait. Colleagues quietly move other patients away. She records the incident and what helped, so the care plan can avoid the same flashpoint.

teach.caption: NG10 rec 1.4.5: use a restrictive intervention only if de-escalation and other strategies, including p.r.n. medication, have failed and there is potential for harm if no action is taken.

No pressure on rib cage, neck or abdomen; mouth and nose clear
Do not routinely restrain for more than 10 minutes

Proportionate, reasonable, for the shortest time possible
Monitor physical and mental health; immediate debrief
teach.caption: NICE NG10 recs 1.4.23–1.4.33 and 1.4.55. Outside mental health law, the Mental Capacity Act s6 only covers restraint you reasonably believe is necessary to prevent harm and that is proportionate to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm.

teach.caption: RCUK 2025 First aid (suicidal thoughts). NICE NG225: do not use risk scales to decide care; focus on needs and safety planning.

teach.text: Asking someone directly whether they are thinking of suicide does not put the idea in their head; it opens the door to help. And restraint is never the first response to shouting: verbal aggression with no immediate risk of harm calls for de-escalation, not hands-on intervention.

items: De-escalate first: one lead communicator, space, calm voice, respect, choices (NG10).
Look for unmet needs behind behaviour: pain, constipation or urinary retention, fear, sensory loss (CG103).
Restrictive interventions only when de-escalation and p.r.n. have failed and harm is likely; never to punish.
Manual restraint: no pressure on chest, neck or abdomen; prone as briefly as possible; not routinely over 10 minutes.
After rapid tranquillisation: observations at least hourly, every 15 minutes if sedated or higher risk.

summary: You can now de-escalate an agitated person using NG10 principles, look for the unmet need behind behaviour that challenges, and respond to suicidal thoughts by asking directly. You also know the safety rules if restraint or rapid tranquillisation becomes unavoidable.

A.q: Ms Doyle, 38, is shouting at the nurses' station after waiting 3 hours for pain relief. She is not threatening anyone. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Ask security to stand next to her while she is spoken to
Tell her firmly she will be removed if she keeps shouting
Ask two colleagues to hold her arms until she calms down
Acknowledge her frustration and ask about her pain
A.why: NG10 de-escalation: communicate respect and empathy, respond to anger in a measured way, avoid provocation and seek to resolve the cause (here, delayed pain relief).

whyNot.0: Bringing security in when there is no threat can feel confrontational and escalate the situation.
whyNot.1: An ultimatum is a classic flashpoint that may provoke rather than calm.
whyNot.2: Holding her would be a restrictive intervention with no risk of harm to justify it.

A.q: Mr Ferreira, 83, has dementia and has started hitting out during personal care each evening. He cannot describe how he feels. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask for p.r.n. sedation to be given before personal care
Assess for pain, constipation and other unmet needs
Arrange for three staff to hold him during washing
Stop personal care until his behaviour has settled
A.why: NICE CG103 asks nurses to assess for pain, including non-verbal signs in people with communication difficulties such as dementia (rec 1.4.9), and to address constipation (rec 1.4.5). Distress during care often reflects an unmet need like this: find and treat the cause first.

whyNot.0: Sedation does not address the cause and medication should follow, not replace, assessment.
whyNot.2: Holding him is restrictive and may increase distress; it does not find the cause.
whyNot.3: Stopping care risks neglect of hygiene and skin and still leaves the cause unknown.

A.q: Tom, 29, tells a nurse on a surgical ward that he has been thinking about ending his life. What is the most appropriate first response?
options: Ask him directly about his thoughts and any plans
Change the subject to avoid making the thoughts any worse
Reassure him that things will look better after his surgery
Complete a suicide risk scale to decide on his level of risk
A.why: RCUK 2025 first aid: ask about suicidal thoughts, explore any plans and listen non-judgementally. NICE NG225 advises against using risk scales to decide care.

whyNot.1: Avoiding the topic leaves him unsupported; asking directly does not increase risk.
whyNot.2: Premature reassurance dismisses his distress and may stop him talking.
whyNot.3: NICE NG225 says risk scales should not be used to predict suicide or decide care.

B.q: On an acute mental health ward, Daniel, 24, is being manually restrained after hitting a nurse. He has been taken to the floor face down. Which action is the priority for the nurse leading?
options: Keep him prone until the doctor arrives to review him
Ask a colleague to kneel across his back to keep him still
Monitor his airway and breathing and turn him face up soon
Cover his face with a towel to stop him spitting at staff
B.why: NG10: if prone restraint is needed use it for as short a time as possible, prefer supine, avoid any pressure on the rib cage, neck or abdomen and ensure someone monitors airway, breathing and vital signs.

whyNot.0: Prone restraint should last as short a time as possible, not until a review.
whyNot.1: Pressure on the back or rib cage restricts breathing and is specifically advised against.
whyNot.3: Obstructing the face interferes with breathing and communication, which NG10 prohibits.

B.q: Mrs Ahmed, 52, received IM lorazepam for rapid tranquillisation 20 minutes ago. She is now asleep. Under NICE NG10, how often should her observations be taken?
options: At least every hour until there are no further concerns
At least every 15 minutes, as she appears to be sedated
Every 4 hours, as for any other inpatient on the ward
Once she wakes, so that her sleep is not disturbed
B.why: NG10 rec 1.4.45: monitor at least hourly after rapid tranquillisation, but every 15 minutes if the person appears to be asleep or sedated.

whyNot.0: Hourly is the minimum, but sedation triggers 15-minute monitoring.
whyNot.2: 4-hourly observations miss early respiratory depression after IM sedation.
whyNot.3: Sedation is exactly when monitoring matters most; it should not wait until she wakes.

B.q: Which statement about restrictive interventions is consistent with NICE NG10?
options: They may be used after any verbal threat to keep staff safe
They may be used when the person has refused to take p.r.n.
They follow failed de-escalation and p.r.n. when harm is likely
They may be used as a consequence to discourage repeat behaviour
B.why: NG10 rec 1.4.5: only if de-escalation and other preventive strategies including p.r.n. medication have failed and there is potential for harm. Rec 1.4.6: never to punish.

whyNot.0: A verbal threat calls for de-escalation; restriction needs failed de-escalation and likely harm.
whyNot.1: Refusing p.r.n. alone does not justify restriction without potential for harm.
whyNot.3: NG10 prohibits restrictive interventions as punishment or to establish dominance.

C.q: Mrs Okoye, 79, has delirium on a medical ward and keeps trying to pull out her cannula. She lacks capacity to decide about the cannula, which is needed for IV antibiotics. A colleague suggests holding her hands down whenever she reaches for it. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, when is restraint lawful?
options: When it prevents harm and is proportionate to that harm
When the next of kin has agreed to the restraint in writing
When it is written into the care plan by the senior nurse
When the person lacks capacity and the team agrees it is best
C.why: MCA s6: restraint is only protected if the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to P and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. Less restrictive options (hiding or re-siting the cannula, oral antibiotics) should be tried.

whyNot.1: Relatives cannot consent to restraint for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA, and s6 conditions still apply.
whyNot.2: A care plan entry does not by itself satisfy the s6 necessity and proportionality tests.
whyNot.3: Lacking capacity and best interests are needed, but s6 adds necessity and proportionality for restraint.

C.q: After a restraint on an inpatient mental health ward, the patient is calm and the immediate risks have been contained. Which action does NICE NG10 recommend next?
options: A written warning to the patient about future behaviour
An immediate debrief including a nurse and a doctor
A formal review by the trust board within 24 hours
Moving the patient to seclusion to prevent a repeat
C.why: NG10 rec 1.4.55: when risks are contained, hold an immediate post-incident debrief including a nurse and a doctor, to address physical harm, ongoing risk and emotional impact on patients and staff, including witnesses.

whyNot.0: A warning is punitive and is not part of NG10 post-incident care.
whyNot.2: Boards receive regular reports, but the first step is an immediate debrief on the ward.
whyNot.3: Seclusion is a further restrictive intervention and is not justified once the patient is calm.

C.q: Aisha, 19, who has a learning disability, becomes very distressed in a busy outpatient waiting area and starts banging her head on the wall. Her support worker says noise is a known trigger. What should the nurse do first?
options: Hold her head still to stop further injury until she calms
Ask her support worker to take her home and rebook later
Give p.r.n. sedation that is prescribed on her records
Move her to a quiet room with her support worker
C.why: NG10: separate the person from the trigger using a quiet area to aid de-escalation, use known triggers and calming strategies from her plan and keep her safe. Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act s20) such as a quiet space should follow.

whyNot.0: Holding her is restrictive and likely to increase distress; removing the trigger comes first.
whyNot.1: Sending her home denies care and does not meet the reasonable adjustment duty.
whyNot.2: Medication is not the first response when a known trigger can be removed.

reteach.title: The volume dial
reteach.question: Think of agitation as a dial being turned up. What turns it down, and what turns it up?

blocks.body: Calm voice, open posture, space, a quiet room, acknowledging feelings and offering real choices turn the dial down. Crowds of staff, ultimatums, arguing, touching without warning and noise turn it up. NG10 calls situations like refusing a request or asking someone to stop doing something 'flashpoints': plan how to handle them so the dial does not jump.

blocks.text: Restriction does not turn the dial down by itself; it is a safety measure of last resort. Keep de-escalating throughout, and debrief afterwards.

explain.body: One staff member takes the lead. Assess safety, give space, use a calm voice and open posture, acknowledge feelings, negotiate and offer choices. Separate the person from others using a quiet area without leaving staff isolated (NG10 1.3.14–1.3.20).

test.q: Under NICE NG10, who should communicate with an agitated person?
options: Every member of staff present
The most senior doctor available
One staff member in the lead
The security team on duty
test.why: NG10 rec 1.3.18: one staff member should take the primary role in communicating, assessing safety and negotiating.

whyNot.0: Several voices at once can confuse and escalate.
whyNot.1: Seniority is not the criterion; one clear lead communicator is.
whyNot.3: Security may support safety, but de-escalation is led by one staff member.

explain.body: Behaviour that challenges often signals pain, discomfort, fear, hunger, thirst, a full bladder or rectum, or sensory loss. Look for non-verbal signs of pain (CG103 rec 1.4.9) and use a behavioural pain tool if the person cannot report pain: UK guidance on pain in older people (2018) recommends PAINAD or Doloplus-2, and the Abbey scale is widely used.

test.q: Which is the best first step when Mrs Rowe, who has dementia, becomes newly agitated at night?
options: Request p.r.n. sedation
Raise the bed rails
Move her bed nearer the station
Check for pain and retention
test.why: New agitation in a person with dementia may reflect unrelieved pain, constipation or urinary retention; CG103 asks for assessment of pain (rec 1.4.9) and constipation (rec 1.4.5), so assess and treat causes first.

whyNot.0: Sedation before assessment risks missing a treatable cause.
whyNot.1: Bed rails can cause entrapment and falls if she climbs and need a risk assessment.
whyNot.2: Closer observation may help, but it does not identify the cause.

explain.body: Only if de-escalation and p.r.n. have failed and harm is likely. Avoid the floor; supine if possible, prone as briefly as possible; no pressure on rib cage, neck or abdomen; not routinely over 10 minutes; one leader; monitor airway, breathing and vital signs.

test.q: Under NICE NG10, staff carrying out manual restraint must avoid applying pressure to which part of the body?
options: The upper arms
The rib cage
The wrists
The lower legs
test.why: NG10 rec 1.4.25: do not use manual restraint in a way that interferes with airway, breathing or circulation, for example by applying pressure to the rib cage, neck or abdomen, or obstructing the mouth or nose.

whyNot.0: Holding the upper arms is a recognised restraint hold; NG10 1.4.25 names the rib cage, neck and abdomen because pressure there restricts breathing.
whyNot.2: Supporting the wrists does not compress the chest; the NG10 warning covers the rib cage, neck and abdomen.
whyNot.3: Holding the lower legs does not restrict breathing; NG10 1.4.25 warns against pressure on the rib cage, neck or abdomen.

explain.body: Ask directly. Explore whether there is a plan. Listen without judgement. If there is a concrete plan or threat, tell them you are getting help, stay with them and escalate urgently. Do not use risk scales to decide care (NG225).

test.q: Joe says he has a plan to take an overdose tonight. What should the nurse do?
options: Stay with him and get urgent help
Give him a crisis line number
Note it for the next ward round
Ask him to sign a no-harm contract
test.why: RCUK 2025: if there are concrete plans, tell the person you are going to get help and call for urgent assistance; do not leave him alone.

whyNot.1: Signposting suits people without a plan; a concrete plan needs urgent help now.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a ward round leaves him at immediate risk.
whyNot.3: A signed agreement does not reduce the immediate risk; a concrete plan needs urgent help now.
